svg.text: FIG 02: FIRST-ORDER RC & RL TRANSIENTS, MASTER STEP RESPONSE & MULTI-INTERVAL SWITCHING
Differential Equation Formulation • The Universal Master Step Formula • Time Constant Evaluation with Controlled Sources • 5τ Settling Criteria

g.text: Any circuit containing exactly ONE effective energy storage element (or multiple
elements of same type that reduce to a single equivalent) is described by:
• x(t) is any branch voltage or current in the network.
• τ is the characteristic Time Constant of the circuit.
• K is the forcing excitation constant: K = x(∞) / τ.
The time constant τ measures the temporal inertia / sluggishness of the response:
Duality Contrast: Increasing resistance R_th INCREASES τ in RC, but DECREASES τ in RL!
Evaluating R_th Seen by Dynamic Element
R_th is the Thévenin equivalent resistance looking into the network from the
terminals of the energy storage element for t > 0:
1. Temporarily remove the capacitor C or inductor L from the circuit.
2. Deactivate all independent sources (V_s → Short, I_s → Open).
3. Look into the exposed terminals and calculate R_eq via series-parallel combinations.
Series-parallel reduction FAILS! Keep controlled sources active, apply test source:
R_th = V_test / I_test (1 V or 1 A external test source)
• If circuit has dependent sources, τ can be significantly modified or become negative!
Consider discharging curve x(t) = x(0) · e^{-t/τ}:
Initial rate of decay at t = 0:
The tangent line drawn to the transient response curve at t = 0 intersects the
final horizontal steady-state asymptote at EXACTLY t = τ!
If the initial rate of decay were maintained constant without exponential slowing,
the response would reach its final steady-state value in exactly ONE time constant τ!
THE TITAN MASTER STEP RESPONSE FORMULA
In ANY first-order dynamic network with DC sources and switching at t = 0,
EVERY branch voltage and branch current x(t) obeys the universal formula:
To solve ANY first-order problem in 90 seconds, determine only 3 parameters:
• Determine i_L(0⁻) and v_C(0⁻) from DC steady state before switching (t = 0⁻).
• At t = 0⁺, replace L with current source i_L(0⁻) and C with voltage source v_C(0⁻).
• Solve static resistive circuit for target quantity x(0⁺).
• For t ≫ 5τ under new switch topology, replace L with SHORT and C with OPEN.
• Solve static DC resistive circuit for target quantity x(∞).
• For t > 0, look into terminals of storage element with independent sources killed.
• Calculate R_th ⟹ τ = R_th · C (for RC) or τ = L / R_th (for RL).
Uncharged capacitor C in series with R connected to DC voltage V_s at t = 0:
v_R(t) = i(t) · R = V_s · e^{-t/RC} (Notice: v_R(0⁺) = V_s jumps!)
Unenergized inductor L in series with R connected to DC voltage V_s at t = 0:
v_L(0⁺) = V_s - i(0⁺)R = V_s, v_L(∞) = 0 V (inductor shorts!)
v_L(t) = V_s · e^{-t / (L/R)} (Notice: v_L(0⁺) = V_s jumps!)
When a second switching event occurs at t = t₁ > 0 (e.g. switch closes at t = 0
• Evaluate value of state variable at the boundary: x(t₁⁻) = x₁(t₁).
• τ₂ and x(∞₂) are computed using the NEW circuit topology for t > t₁!
Time-Varying Resistor R(t) in Series RC Circuit
If resistance varies with time: R(t) = R₀ · (1 + αt) or R(t) = k·t:
DANGER: Formula x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0) - x(∞)]e^{-t/τ} FAILS because τ is not constant!
Differential equation: R(t) · C · dv_C/dt + v_C(t) = V_s
General solution: v_C(t) = (1 / I.F.) · [ ∫ (V_s / R(t)C) · I.F. dt + K ].
Constant K determined from initial condition v_C(0⁺) = v_C(0⁻)!
Consider an Op-Amp or transistor circuit with controlled source and 1 capacitor:
Step 1: Calculate Thevenin Resistance R_th Seen by C:
• Connect V_test = 1 V across capacitor terminals (with independent sources killed).
• Solve for I_test entering positive terminal: R_th = 1 V / I_test.
τ = R_th · C (May be much smaller or larger than physical resistors!)
Negative Feedback: Reduces effective R_th, dramatically accelerating circuit!
• When driven by a rectangular pulse of width T, capacitor NEVER reaches V_s.
• Peak voltage achieved at end of pulse: V_peak = V_s · [1 - e^{-T/τ}].
• For t > T, discharges from V_peak: v_C(t) = V_peak · e^{-(t - T)/τ}.
If T ≪ τ: Exponential approximates a pure linear ramp: v_C(t) ≈ V_s · (t/τ)!
Time required for response to rise from 10% to 90% of final value:
In electrical power engineering, circuits are assumed in full DC steady state after 5τ.
Consider charging an initially uncharged capacitor C from DC voltage source V_s:
1. Total Energy Delivered by Voltage Source:
E_source = ∫₀^∞ V_s · i(t) dt = V_s · Q_total = C · V_s²
3. Energy Dissipated as Heat in Resistor R:
E_resistor = E_source - E_cap = ½ C · V_s² (Exactly 50% !)
Remarkable Invariant: Dissipation is INDEPENDENT of resistance R!
(Whether R = 1 mΩ or R = 1 MΩ, exactly half the source energy is lost as heat!).
1. Always find state variables i_L(0⁺) and v_C(0⁺) FIRST.
2. Determine R_th seen by storage element AFTER switching (for t > 0).
Never integrate differential equations from scratch when Master Formula applies!
